title: Fear and worldly cares led a covenant maker to break his word
setting: James Covel left Fayette within a day of the 5 January revelation, without explaining why. Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon were left asking why he had not obeyed. Joseph later recalled that this revelation, dated 6 January 1831, gave the reason. His history says Covel returned to his former principles and people.
summary: The revelation says James Covel’s heart had been right, for he covenanted to obey the Lord’s word. He received the word with gladness. It says Satan tempted him straightway. The fear of persecution and the cares of the world led him to reject the word. So he broke the covenant. The revelation leaves his outcome with the Lord, to do “as seemeth me good”.

contextNote.title: How a glad start ended
contextNote.text: Joseph and Sidney wanted to know why a man who promised obedience had walked away. Verse 1 says that his heart had been right and his covenant real. Verse 2 gives the cause in two parts: “the fear of persecution and the cares of the world”. The wording recalls Jesus’s parable of the sower, where seed received with joy withers or is choked. Verse 3 states the result: he “broke my covenant”. In this passage, rejecting the word is the end of a slide that began with temptation right after gladness.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 37–40 uses James Covel’s experience to contrast earthly cares with the riches of eternity. Verse 2 says Satan tempted him “straightway” after he received the word with gladness; what might help a person hold on in that moment?
reviewNote: Read all 3 verses. Official heading gives Fayette, 6 January 1831, to Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon, after Covel returned to his former principles. JSP introduction notes Covel left within a day; date rests on John Whitmer’s heading in Revelation Book 1. The sower comparison in contextNote is my own reading of the wording. Fact-check 2026-10-12: summary and contextNote now attribute Satan's temptation and Covel's right heart to the revelation instead of stating them as fact.
